title: The Fruit of Patience: How Regional Shifts Ripened Turkey's Path to Kurdish Reconciliation
gist: Turkey's parliament passed a disarmament framework law for the Kurdistan Workers' Party days before the Syrian Democratic Forces dissolved, a convergence the authors trace to Erdoğan's domestic need for the pro-Kurdish party's 56 parliamentary votes to renew his term, Öcalan's personal authority over Kurdish commanders, and the collapse of a decade-long U.S.-Kurdish partnership in Syria — but the settlement remains a conditional arms deal, not a constitutional guarantee, and could unravel like the 2015 peace process did.

themes.theme: Domestic political arithmetic drives the reconciliation

insights.claim: Under Turkey's constitution, President Erdoğan can only run for re-election if the constitution changes or parliament votes (needing 360 of 600 members under Article 116) to renew elections; the governing parties fall short of that threshold, and the pro-Kurdish Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party's 56 deputies could supply the missing votes, making Kurdish reconciliation a precondition for Erdoğan's political survival.
insights.speaker: Riccardo Gasco and Samuele C. A. Abrami
insights.so_what: Identifies the precise vote-count mechanism (360/600, 56 swing deputies) explaining why Erdoğan is pursuing Kurdish reconciliation now — a concrete lens for predicting how durable the peace process will be tied to his re-election timeline.
insights.quote: Article 116 requires 360 of parliament’s 600 members to support renewal. The governing parties fall short of that threshold. And the liberal Kurdish-aligned Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party’s 56 deputies could supply the missing votes.
insights.locator: The Arithmetic of a Third Term

insights.claim: Erdoğan's crackdown on the opposition — an appeals court annulling the Republican People's Party leadership contest in May, the imprisonment of Istanbul mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu since March, and a July split that saw 91 deputies leave the party — weakened the main partner the pro-Kurdish party might have used to build an alternative governing coalition, making outreach to Erdoğan more attractive to Kurdish politicians and refusal more costly.
insights.speaker: Riccardo Gasco and Samuele C. A. Abrami
insights.so_what: Shows the reconciliation is a byproduct of engineered opposition weakness rather than genuine political liberalization — a signal that Turkish domestic political risk (opposition suppression) and the Kurdish settlement are mechanically linked, relevant to Turkey country-risk assessments.
insights.quote: Repression made outreach more useful to Erdoğan and refusal more costly for Kurdish politicians.
insights.locator: The Kurdish question has long been the opposition's kryptonite.

insights.claim: June polling showed 68% of Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party voters opposed a continued Turkish military presence in Syria, compared with 38.2% nationally, indicating the emerging Erdoğan-Kurdish alignment is a marriage of immediate political interest rather than shared policy vision, especially on Syria.
insights.speaker: Riccardo Gasco and Samuele C. A. Abrami
insights.so_what: A specific polling gap (68% vs. 38.2%) foreshadowing where the Erdoğan-Kurdish coalition could fracture — a leading indicator to watch for Turkish policy shifts on troop presence in Syria.
insights.quote: June polling showed that 68 percent of Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party voters opposed a continued Turkish military presence in Syria, compared with 38.2 percent nationally.
insights.locator: Still, Erdoğan has kept his distance.

insights.claim: Erdoğan is deliberately keeping political distance from the Kurdish concessions because his coalition still depends on the Nationalist Movement Party (chaired by Devlet Bahçeli), and legislation grants state authority over concessions without making Erdoğan their personal guarantor, preserving his ability to retreat if nationalist backlash grows.
insights.speaker: Riccardo Gasco and Samuele C. A. Abrami
insights.so_what: Explains a structural fragility in the peace process: it has no single political owner willing to be held accountable if it fails, making abrupt reversal easier than in a treaty-based settlement.
insights.quote: Legislation gives the concessions state authority without making the president their personal guarantor, leaving him room to retreat if the political cost rises.
insights.locator: Still, Erdoğan has kept his distance.

themes.theme: The end of the U.S.-Kurdish partnership in Syria

insights.claim: The Syrian Democratic Forces' decade-long partnership with Washington (since 2014-2015) was narrowly scoped to defeating the Islamic State and never became a political guarantee; American forces left Syria in April 2026, and on August 24, 2026 the U.S. rescinded Syria's state sponsor of terrorism designation, marking a full pivot to the new al-Sharaa government in Damascus.
insights.speaker: Riccardo Gasco and Samuele C. A. Abrami
insights.so_what: Documents the concrete timeline (April 2026 withdrawal, August 24 2026 terrorism-designation rescission) by which U.S. leverage in Syria was spent — relevant to assessing U.S. influence over any future minority-rights enforcement in Syria's new constitution.
insights.quote: When Washington judged the mission complete, American forces left Syria in April. On Aug. 24, the United States rescinded Syria’s designation as a state sponsor of terrorism
insights.locator: Washington began working with Kurdish-led forces in northeastern Syria in 2014...

insights.claim: Mazloum Abdi announced the dissolution of the Syrian Democratic Forces on August 25, 2026, at the People's Palace in Damascus, saying the force had joined the Syrian army and would no longer operate independently — occurring just 15 days after Turkey's parliament passed its Kurdistan Workers' Party disarmament framework law on August 10.
insights.speaker: Riccardo Gasco and Samuele C. A. Abrami
insights.so_what: Establishes the precise causal linkage (law passed Aug 10, dissolution announced Aug 25) tying the Turkish and Syrian Kurdish tracks together as a single coordinated political-military event, not independent developments.
insights.quote: By including affiliated organizations, parliament tied the fate of the Syrian Democratic Forces to the return of fighters from Turkey. The link entered law on Aug. 10, 15 days before Abdi announced the dissolution in Damascus.
insights.locator: The Last Authority of Abdullah Öcalan

insights.claim: Abdullah Öcalan's February 2025 appeal for disarmament — which renounced separate nation-states, federations, administrative autonomy, and 'culturalist solutions' — gave Mazloum Abdi a path to seek terms with Damascus, and Öcalan's personal authority over commanders who served with him in Syria before his 1998 expulsion made the compressed settlement timeline possible; however, this authority is personal, finite, and cannot pass automatically to a successor or institution.
insights.speaker: Riccardo Gasco and Samuele C. A. Abrami
insights.so_what: A key single-point-of-failure risk: the entire reconciliation architecture depends on one aging, imprisoned individual's personal authority, which has no institutional successor — a major durability risk investors/analysts should flag for the settlement's longevity.
insights.quote: His authority over commanders who had served with him in Syria before his expulsion in 1998 allowed him to move Kurdish leaders toward a common course after decades in prison... his authority is personal, finite, and cannot pass automatically to a successor or an institution.
insights.locator: The Last Authority of Abdullah Öcalan

themes.theme: A settlement of arms, not of the Kurdish question

insights.claim: The authors' central thesis is that what emerged between Turkey and Kurdish actors is 'a settlement of arms, not yet a settlement of the Kurdish question' — no treaty, independent guarantor, or constitutional protection was produced, and it remains vulnerable to the same political and strategic volatility that made it possible.
insights.speaker: Riccardo Gasco and Samuele C. A. Abrami
insights.so_what: The core investable/analytical takeaway: treat this reconciliation as a fragile ceasefire-style arrangement rather than a resolved conflict — geopolitical risk in Turkey/Syria/northern Iraq remains elevated pending constitutional follow-through.
insights.quote: What emerged is a settlement of arms, not yet a settlement of the Kurdish question, and it remains vulnerable to the political and strategic volatility that made it possible.
insights.locator: In 2024, we correctly saw the growing interconnection...

insights.claim: Turkey's disarmament law is structured so that Turkish security institutions and a president-chaired National Security Council alone verify compliance and decide when legal benefits (suspended sentences over 5-10 year probation) begin, meaning the state is simultaneously a party to the process and its judge, with no independent monitoring commission like the one Ankara rejected in 2015.
insights.speaker: Riccardo Gasco and Samuele C. A. Abrami
insights.so_what: Highlights the absence of independent verification as a structural weakness that could allow the Turkish state to unilaterally stall or reverse implementation — a legal/political risk factor for the durability of the reconciliation.
insights.quote: The state is both a party to the process and its judge.

insights.claim: The 2015 Turkish-Kurdish peace process comparison shows that 'ripeness does not last': domestic and external pressures can align actors and then pull them apart when the balance shifts, meaning the current convergence is a favorable moment rather than a durable achievement.
insights.speaker: Riccardo Gasco and Samuele C. A. Abrami
insights.so_what: A general framework (ripeness vs. achievement) for evaluating any conflict-resolution process shaped by transient alignment of interests rather than institutionalized guarantees — applicable beyond this specific case.
insights.quote: The comparison with 2015 shows why ripeness does not last. Domestic and external pressures can bring actors together and then pull them apart when the balance shifts.
insights.locator: The comparison with 2015 shows why ripeness does not last.

insights.claim: Syria's Kurdish concessions (citizenship for stateless Kurds, Kurdish-language teaching, senior state roles) are individual offices and rights granted from the center rather than binding constitutional protections, and the Syrian state has not yet shown it can protect minorities — mob attacks and reprisals continue largely unprosecuted, and new security services remain mostly Sunni with minority recruits in administrative or unarmed roles.
insights.speaker: Riccardo Gasco and Samuele C. A. Abrami
insights.so_what: A concrete red flag on Syria's post-Assad governance capacity that bears on any assessment of Syria's stability for reconstruction investment or aid disbursement.
insights.quote: A government that cannot yet protect Alawites, Druze, and Christians cannot secure Kurdish rights through decrees alone.
insights.locator: That gap matters because the Syrian state has not shown...

themes.theme: Regional disorder and the limits of Kurdish leverage

insights.claim: During the 2026 U.S./Israel-Iran war, Iranian Kurdish armed groups based in Iraq offered Washington organized cross-border networks as a possible ground component against Tehran, but Iraqi Kurdish leaders resisted (fearing Iranian retaliation) and Turkish officials pressured U.S. officials to discourage intervention; by March 7, Trump told Kurdish forces to stay out, and Iran's foreign minister later credited Ankara with helping prevent a new front.
insights.speaker: Riccardo Gasco and Samuele C. A. Abrami
insights.so_what: Demonstrates Turkey's demonstrated capability to shape U.S. military decisions in the region by leveraging its relationship with Kurdish actors — a data point on Ankara's regional influence relevant to any U.S.-Iran escalation scenario analysis.
insights.quote: By March 7, Trump was telling Kurdish forces to stay out, and Iran’s foreign minister later credited Ankara with helping prevent a new front.
insights.locator: The Trump administration discussed operations in western Iran...

insights.claim: The authors argue that drones, surveillance, and precision weapons have structurally weakened the classic guerrilla model of using terrain, concealment, and time to outlast stronger states, and that Turkey spent a decade applying these tools against the Kurdistan Workers' Party in Iraq and Syria, limiting its ability to hide and regroup — reducing overall Kurdish strategic leverage even as regional disorder temporarily raised it.
insights.speaker: Riccardo Gasco and Samuele C. A. Abrami
insights.so_what: A broader causal claim about how drone/surveillance technology structurally disadvantages non-state insurgent groups relative to states — a transferable framework for assessing other asymmetric conflicts (e.g., Sahel, Myanmar).
insights.quote: Guerrilla forces once used terrain, concealment, and time to outlast stronger states. Drones, surveillance, and precision weapons have weakened that model.
insights.locator: Military change narrowed the opportunity further.

source_meta.author: Riccardo Gasco and Samuele C. A. Abrami
